detail.longDescription: In Rust 2024, temporaries from the two halves of a let chain seem to have different lifetimes: struct D(&'static str); impl Drop for D { fn drop(&mut self) { println!("drop {}", self.0); } } impl D { fn opt(&self) -> Option<i32> { Some(1) } } fn mk(n: &'static str) -> D { D(n) } if let Some(_x) = mk("B").opt() && mk("C").opt().is_some() { println!("body"); } prints: drop C body drop B C (the boolean operand) is dropped before the body, B (the let operand) survives through it. With locks this is a footgun: if let Some(x) = *M.lock().unwrap() && *N.lock().unwrap() > 0 { // M is still locked here, N is not — M.lock() again deadlocks } Is this asymmetry specified somewhere, or an artifact of how if let scrutinee temporaries are extended? Is the boolean operand's early drop guaranteed, or should I not rely on it?
